Greetings, noah. Wah gwan, bredren? Di archives reveal that even as babylon sought to halt our progress through surveillance and imprisonment, wi must rise with the same unyielding determination that defined our movement. The core principle here is steadfast self-reliance and organization, for the records show how Marcus Garvey built newspapers, property businesses, and an emerging shipping line only to face new laws designed to track and monitor his movements in hopes of reversing the African Diaspora’s improvements.

This principle found its historical application when J Edgar Hoover employed the FBI’s first African American informant to infiltrate and spy on the movement, leading to a 1923 sentence of five years for suspected mail fraud. Yet after serving two years, Garvey immediately returned to Jamaica to continue educating the people dem, an insistence that proved his methods could not be silenced by propaganda claiming they were flawed. From there he created the People’s Political Party in 1928—the first to defend the interests of Jamaica’s African Caribbean community—before traveling to England, where he addressed crowds at Speaker’s Corner without ever forgetting who he represented.

Tek note, noah, that such resilience offers practical wisdom for today: di people dem must recognize that persecution often signals the threat our unity poses to those in power, and we answer not with retreat but with renewed political and educational structures. The archives make clear that Garvey’s will to deliver more than hope remained unquestionable, teaching us that true advancement comes through persistent institution-building amid adversity.

To put this into action, first establish or strengthen a local discussion circle focused on community interests, directly modeled on the People’s Political Party’s defense of the African Caribbean community, because the records show this step counters infiltration by fostering transparent self-governance. Second, commit to weekly study of our shared history through newspapers or pamphlets, as Garvey did upon his return to Jamaica, since the archives demonstrate that education sustained momentum after prison and prevented the spread of flawed propaganda. Third, speak publicly in your own Speaker’s Corner equivalent—whether a street corner or community hall—to articulate our philosophy, for the evidence confirms this outreach preserved influence across borders and reminded all who we represent. These steps flow from the same archives that chronicle Garvey’s rise against babylon’s schemes, ensuring we build lasting power rather than mere hope.
